title: Mortality among cocaine users: A systematic review of cohort studies

claims.statement: In seven cohorts of people with problematic or dependent cocaine use, followed between 1985 and 2005 in the USA (two cohorts), Canada, France, the Netherlands, Brazil and Italy and summarized without pooling in one systematic review (Degenhardt et al., 2011; figures second-hand, several of them supplied by the cohorts' investigators as personal communications), deaths were 4.4 to 7.7 times as frequent as in the general population of the same age and sex in the four cohorts that reported standardized mortality ratios (SMR): 4.74 (95% CI 4.19 to 5.29) among 717 people injecting cocaine in Vancouver; 4.36 among men and 7.70 among women in a French national cohort of 2212 people arrested for using or dealing cocaine or crack; 4.75 (2.26 to 9.96) among men in treatment for cocaine dependence in Italy (mostly intranasal use by one of the review's two descriptions, crack dependence by the other); and 7.60 at five years among 131 people treated for crack dependence in São Paulo. Crude death rates ranged from about 0.5 to 6.2 per 100 person-years, that is about 5 to 62 deaths per 1,000 people per year: 6.16 in the Vancouver cohort; 4.69 among people injecting cocaine only and 4.37 among people injecting cocaine and heroin in Baltimore; 4.6 among HIV-negative people mainly injecting cocaine in the Netherlands (9 deaths); 3.51 in the São Paulo crack cohort and 3.53 among people smoking crack daily in Seattle (3 deaths); and 0.69 in the French arrest cohort and 0.50 in the Italian treatment cohort. Where it was examined, death rates were about twice as high in people with HIV (Vancouver 9.83 against 4.91 per 100 person-years; Baltimore 7.74 and 7.98 against 3.25 and 3.45). The leading causes of death were AIDS, overdose and injuries among people who injected (Baltimore, people injecting cocaine only: AIDS 62 of 175 deaths, overdose 20, sepsis or endocarditis 15, injuries 12, heart disease 7, suicide 2; Vancouver: overdose 53, AIDS 30 and injuries 23 of 158 deaths), gunshot wounds (10 of 23 deaths) and AIDS (6) among people treated for crack dependence in Brazil, and, in the Italian cohort of 309 men with 7 deaths, cause-specific SMRs of 14.85 (4.79 to 46.04) for vascular disease, 9.95 (1.40 to 70.61) for overdose and 7.07 (1 to 50.16) for suicide. The SMRs take only age and sex into account, so they describe the excess deaths in these groups, not an effect of cocaine itself apart from injecting, HIV, heroin and alcohol use and social disadvantage, which the authors name as possible reasons for the differences. All the cohorts came from injecting, treatment or arrest settings, mostly socially disadvantaged and several with high HIV prevalence, the effect of HIV treatment could not be examined, and no cohort followed people who only snort cocaine (the authors think it likely, citing another study, that their mortality is much lower, but there are no data). How deaths were identified and causes assigned is not reported for the cohorts, and the review's table has inconsistencies: the lowest crude rate printed (0.53, for people injecting daily in Seattle) does not match its own 3 deaths in 319 person-years, which give 0.94 (editors' calculation).
claims.magnitude: Second-hand, not pooled. SMR against the general population of the same age and sex (4 cohorts): 4.74 (4.19 to 5.29), people injecting cocaine, Vancouver; 4.36 (men) and 7.70 (women), people arrested for cocaine offences, France; 4.75 (2.26 to 9.96), men in treatment, Italy; 7.60 at 5 years, people treated for crack dependence, São Paulo. Crude mortality about 0.5 to 6.2 per 100 person-years (about 5 to 62 per 1,000 per year), by cohort as in the statement; with HIV 9.83 against 4.91 (Vancouver) and 7.7 to 8.0 against 3.3 to 3.5 (Baltimore) per 100 person-years. Causes as in the statement.
